tweets.text: I don’t disagree that “reducing inflation works if it’s tried”. I do disagree that trying it singularly with monetary policy while fiscal policy rows in the other direction is a fool’s errand. Maybe hiking 2 times of 25bps each will do wonders. I somehow rather doubt it. You’d need a lot more if the goal is to reach 2% quickly. I don’t see where you’d get that type of realistic political capital for the Fed. So maybe doing something is better than doing nothing except doing something makes the other factors feel like the Fed has got it under control while they could go on doing whatever they were doing.

Re: $Pons discussions. Someone sent me this chart asking my thoughts. While it's true that CT tends to extrapolate revenue out waaayyy too far into the future. I do think it has a chance to be sticky. Most the people who are saying that, didn't participate in any upside.

At least people are trading a token that has some underlying value. Yes, it's unlikely the revenues will be sustained at that pace. But it doesnt mean it can't go on longer. And it doesnt mean there aren't risks like competitors coming to the chain etc. There are of course a ton of risks. Lots of things trade higher, and they have ZERO value. 

In general, the market is a giant pendulum that swings to extremes. I for one, am happy for the volatility in general. That's what we are here for. Maybe this time is different, idk. Is it overvalued? Nobody knows. Are they killing it? yes. Will they always? Maybe not. in short, the chart is a good example of the past, but a very limited sample size. 

I think we will see it swing to extremes each way in terms of over and undervalued. Imo, just enjoy the volatility and make the most of it

#Copper #Uranium #Silver #Gold

DAILY METALS PULSE — September 8, 2026

SEASONALITY IS KICKING IN, AND IT IS ARRIVING ON TOP OF ALREADY STRONG FUNDAMENTALS.

September begins an important seasonal handover:

• Indian festival and wedding demand starts building for gold and silver.
• China enters its traditional “Golden September, Silver October” industrial-demand period, supporting copper.
• Uranium emerges from its summer slowdown as utilities, producers and fuel buyers return to the contracting market.

Seasonality never guarantees a rally, but it becomes powerful when physical markets are already tightening.

🟠 COPPER

LME copper hit a fresh all-time high of $14,533/tonne.

Global mine production fell 1.1% in H1, while concentrate output dropped 2.6%. U.S. tariff fears are also pulling metal into America and reducing availability elsewhere.

Now the record breakout is coinciding with China’s traditional autumn restocking and manufacturing period.

Copper in the wrong warehouse is not available supply—and seasonal demand is arriving.

🟡 GOLD

Gold gained 0.6% to approximately $4,433 as the dollar weakened.

The immediate test is this week’s U.S. PPI and CPI data, with markets pricing roughly a 60% probability of another Fed hike. Yet gold continues to absorb that hawkish pressure remarkably well.

Indian festival and wedding buying should now provide an additional seasonal tailwind into Q4. High prices may constrain jewellery volumes, but investment buying and restocking can remain strong.

⚪ SILVER

Silver rose 1.2% to around $66.96, outperforming gold and reducing the gold–silver ratio to approximately 66.

Silver may have the most interesting seasonal setup of all: it can benefit from precious-metals buying in India while simultaneously gaining from the post-summer recovery in industrial activity.

When gold demand, copper strength and silver seasonality align, moves can accelerate quickly.

☢️ URANIUM

Uranium remains firm near $89.50/lb, up more than 17% year over year.

The market is now emerging from its typical summer lull. Contracting activity tends to improve from September as utilities and fuel-cycle participants return, with the World Nuclear Symposium beginning tomorrow.

Around 80 reactors are under construction globally and another 120 are planned. The long-term requirement for secure uranium supply continues to grow while uncovered utility needs accumulate.

THE TAKE:

Seasonality is not creating the bullish thesis. It is arriving on top of it.

Copper is breaking into price discovery. Gold is holding despite hawkish rate expectations. Silver is regaining leverage. Uranium is entering its post-summer contracting period just below $90.

Four metals. Four tightening markets. And now the calendar is becoming a tailwind.

Easiest way to happiness is to figure out what makes a great day for you. 

And try to create the environment and routines to make the happy days more consistent. 

Some things for me (as an Unc with no kids):

• Waking up without an alarm
• 3-4 hours of deep work in the morning
• Afternoon workout
• Spending time with A.I. to automate more stuff / build leverage
• Cut as many meetings as possible
• Cooking at dinner at home on the weekdays
• Unscheduled evening time. Meet up with people, side projects, video games, etc.
• Be in bed by 10pm

I love days like this, but I would’ve HATED it a decade ago.

Something that really helped me was to keep a simple journal. At the end of everyday just grade your day on how much you enjoy it, and look for patterns.

Whatever you liked, keep repeating. Whatever you hate, do less.

A happy life is a bunch of happy days, so just figure out what makes a great day.

tweets.text:
Very few people will actually notice the step change from GPT 5.6 to GPT 6 Astra. The reason is simple: most everyday tasks are already saturated. AI is already at 100%.

I can ask ChatGPT to find the email of a babysitter, email her, send a calendar invite, then text my wife. Or take a photo of my bike tire, have it identify the exact tire, research it, and tell me the right PSI.

It already does all of this extremely well. There is no 120%.So if I switch to Astra, I may see almost 0 difference. Maybe it is faster and cheaper, but with a subscription you barely feel either.

The capability jump will be obvious if you are at the frontier of coding, math or science. For everyone else, AI has become so good that the next huge leap might feel surprisingly invisible.
